standard_text: Show that the distance between two rational numbers on the number line is the absolute value of their difference, and apply this principle in real-world contexts.

progression.narrative:
This standard turns subtraction into a story about distance. The distance between two numbers on the number line is the absolute value of their difference, |a - b| — and because distance can never be negative, the absolute value is doing essential work. So the arc begins by settling absolute value itself: |x| is how far x is from zero, always non-negative. That idea, |-7| = 7, is the anchor.

From there the standard builds the subtraction mechanic that makes the distance formula run. The move students most need is 'add the opposite': a - b becomes a + (-b), which quietly converts every subtraction into the signed addition they already know. The trickiest case is subtracting a negative — 3.5 - (-2.5) — where the two minus signs turn into a plus and the result grows. Fractions and decimals raise the number difficulty without changing the logic. Then students find distance as |a - b| directly, and apply it to contexts: how far a temperature fell, the gap between an elevation above and below sea level, the change in a bank balance. The capstone reasons abstractly about a - b = c from positions on a number line. The through-line we keep naming: subtracting is adding the opposite, and the distance between two numbers is the absolute value of that difference.

steps.rationale: Absolute value is the distance from zero, always non-negative. Reading |x| off a number line is the anchor idea the whole distance principle depends on.
Computing |x| for any rational number makes absolute value automatic before it is used inside the distance formula.
The standard's headline: the distance between two rationals is |a - b|. Students compute this gap, using absolute value so the answer is never negative.
The computational engine: subtract rationals by adding the opposite, a - b = a + (-b). Subtracting a negative (the double-negative case) is the dominant hurdle.
The At-proficiency demand: apply signed subtraction to real-world contexts — temperature drops, elevation gaps, balance changes — and interpret the result.
The Above-proficiency synthesis: reason about a - b = c from positions on a number line, connecting difference, distance, and sign.

skills.name: Place and compare rational numbers on a number line

prerequisite_skill.description: Order positive and negative rationals and place them correctly on a number line.

skills.i_do_script: On a number line, numbers get bigger as you move RIGHT and smaller as you move LEFT. That means for negatives, the one closer to zero is bigger. Watch: -2 and -5. -2 is closer to zero (to the right), so -2 is greater than -5. It feels backwards because 5 is bigger than 2, but with a minus sign, farther left is smaller.

canonical_error.pattern: Orders negative numbers by their size as if they were positive
canonical_error.why: The student compares the digits and ignores the sign. On the number line, a negative farther from zero is smaller, so -5 is less than -2.

skills.item_template: Two or more rationals to compare or order, including negatives. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: Which is greater, -5 or -2?
Order from least to greatest: -3, 1, -0.5.
Which is less, -1/2 or -3/4?
True or false: -8 < -3.
Which is farther RIGHT on a number line, -6 or -1?

redirect_script.stop: Which one is closer to zero?
redirect_script.prompt: On a number line, right is bigger. For negatives, the one closer to zero is greater. Picture -2 and -5: -2 sits to the right, so it's larger.
redirect_script.praise: You used the number line, not just the digits — that's how to order negatives.

vocabulary.definition: A line where numbers increase to the right and decrease to the left.
Any number expressible as a fraction, including integers and decimals.

worked_example_script.text: Mark -4 and -1 on a number line.
Which is farther right? Which is closer to zero?
-1 is farther right and closer to zero, so -1 > -4, even though 4 is bigger than 1.
If a student says -4 > -1, ask 'would you rather owe $4 or $1? Which is the bigger number?'
Your turn: which is greater, -7 or -3?

skills.name: Add a signed number

prerequisite_skill.description: Add two rationals with the same or opposite signs (from 7.NS.1).

skills.i_do_script: Subtraction is going to become addition, so I need signed addition solid. Same signs: add the sizes, keep the sign. Opposite signs: subtract the sizes, keep the sign of the number farther from zero. Watch: -6 + 4 — opposite signs, subtract 6 - 4 = 2, and -6 is farther, so -2. And -6 + (-4) — same signs, -10.

canonical_error.pattern: Applies same-sign rules to opposite signs (or vice versa)
canonical_error.example: For -6 + 4 writes -10 (adding) instead of -2, or for -6 + (-4) writes -2 (subtracting) instead of -10
canonical_error.why: The student doesn't first check whether the signs match. Same signs combine; opposite signs partly cancel.

skills.item_template: A signed addition (same or opposite signs). Short response fluency bank.

redirect_script.stop: Same signs or opposite signs first?
redirect_script.prompt: Check the signs before anything. Same: add and keep the sign. Opposite: subtract and keep the farther number's sign.
redirect_script.praise: You checked the signs first — that's the key to signed addition.

vocabulary.definition: A number with a positive or negative sign.
A number's distance from zero, its size without the sign.

worked_example_script.text: Write '-9 + 5.'
Are the signs the same or opposite? Which number is farther from zero?
Opposite. 9 - 5 = 4, and -9 is farther, so -4.
If a student writes -14, ask 'do opposite signs combine or cancel?'
Your turn: -3 + 8, then -3 + (-8).

skills.name: Interpret absolute value as distance from zero
skills.i_do_script: Absolute value is how FAR a number is from zero — and distance is never negative. The bars |...| ask 'how far from zero?' Watch a point at -3 1/2. Its distance from zero is 3 1/2, so |-3 1/2| = 3 1/2. The value itself is negative, but its distance from zero is positive. Absolute value strips the sign and reports the distance.

canonical_error.pattern: Reports the absolute value of a negative as negative, keeping the sign
canonical_error.why: The student reads the bars as 'copy the number' rather than 'distance from zero.' Distance is always non-negative, so the sign is dropped.

skills.item_template: A number line point or a value; student identifies its absolute value (distance from zero). MC/short response.

sample_items.stem: Point A is at -3 1/2. Which value shows its distance from zero?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Distance from zero is 3 1/2 (positive). The negative options give a negative 'distance.'

sample_items.stem: What is the distance from zero of the number -6?
Which is true about |x| for any number x?
sample_items.answer: It is never negative (distance from zero).
choices: It is never negative (distance from zero)
sample_items.distractor_logic: Absolute value is a non-negative distance; it equals x only when x >= 0.

sample_items.stem: A point is 4.2 units to the left of zero. What is its absolute value?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Distance from zero is 4.2 regardless of side.

redirect_script.prompt: Absolute value asks 'how far from zero?' Distance is never negative, so drop the sign: |-3 1/2| is 3 1/2. Read the bars as 'distance,' not 'copy.'
redirect_script.praise: You read the bars as distance from zero — that's absolute value.

vocabulary.definition: A number's distance from zero; always zero or positive, written |x|.
How far a point is from 0, ignoring direction.

worked_example_script.text: Mark -5 on a number line and write |-5|.
How far is -5 from zero?
5 units. So |-5| = 5. The bars report the distance, which is positive.
If a student writes |-5| = -5, ask 'is a distance ever negative?'
Your turn: what is |-2.75|?

practice_problems.stem: What is |-4|?
Can absolute value ever be negative?
practice_problems.answer: No — it's a distance from zero.

practice_problems.stem: What is |-3 1/2|?
A point is at -6. What is its distance from zero?
Ella evaluated |-3 1/2|. Find and fix her mistake.
practice_problems.answer: Absolute value is distance from zero, which is never negative: |-3 1/2| = 3 1/2. Ella just copied the number with its sign.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: keeping the sign inside absolute value.

practice_problems.stem: What is |8|?
practice_problems.notes: Absolute value of a positive is itself.

practice_problems.stem: For what values of x is |x| = x true? For what values is |x| = -x true?
practice_problems.answer: |x| = x when x >= 0 (non-negative); |x| = -x when x <= 0 (non-positive), because -x is then positive.

practice_problems.stem: Two different numbers have the same absolute value, 5. What are they, and how are they related?
practice_problems.answer: 5 and -5 — they are opposites, the same distance from zero on opposite sides.

misconception_redirects.say: Absolute value asks 'how far from zero?' Distance is never negative, so drop the sign: |-3 1/2| is 3 1/2. Read the bars as 'distance,' not 'copy.'
misconception_redirects.praise: You read the bars as distance from zero — that's absolute value.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student mishandles a negative outside the bars, like -|4|.

-7 (inside first, then the outside negative). An answer of 7 misses the outside sign.

Count the distance, ignoring the side.

skills.name: Evaluate the absolute value of a given number
skills.i_do_script: Evaluating an absolute value is quick once I know it means distance from zero. If the number inside is positive, the answer is itself; if it's negative, drop the sign. Watch: |42| = 42, and |-42| = 42. Both are 42 units from zero. When there's a sign OUTSIDE the bars, I do the inside first: -|42| = -(42) = -42.

canonical_error.pattern: Mishandles a sign outside the bars, or negates a positive inside
canonical_error.why: The student doesn't separate the inside from the outside. Evaluate inside the bars first (always non-negative), then apply any sign written outside.

skills.item_template: An absolute-value expression (with or without an outside sign). Numeric response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: What is |42|?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Absolute value of a positive is itself.

sample_items.stem: What is |-42|?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Distance from zero drops the sign.

sample_items.stem: What is -|7|?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Inside first: |7| = 7; then the outside negative gives -7.

sample_items.stem: What is |-3/5|?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Absolute value of a fraction drops the sign.

redirect_script.stop: Is that sign inside the bars or outside?
redirect_script.prompt: Do the inside first — it comes out non-negative. THEN apply any sign written outside the bars. |−7| is 7; −|7| is −7.
redirect_script.praise: You handled inside then outside — that's the order for absolute value.

vocabulary.definition: A number's distance from zero, written |x|; always non-negative.
Find the numerical value of an expression.

worked_example_script.text: What does each equal? Do the inside first each time.
|-12| = 12 (distance). -|12| = -(12) = -12 (inside is 12, then the outside negative).
If a student writes -|12| = 12, ask 'what's the sign sitting outside the bars?'
Your turn: |-20| and -|-20|.

practice_problems.answer: Do the inside first: |9| = 9, then apply the outside negative: -|9| = -9. Ravi ignored the sign outside the bars.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: dropping the outside sign.

practice_problems.stem: What is |-3/5|?

practice_problems.answer: -8 — inside: |-8| = 8; then the outside negative: -(8) = -8.

activities.title: Inside, Then Outside
activities.instructions:
1. Read Ravi's claim that -|9| = 9.
2. Circle what's inside the bars and what's outside.
3. Evaluate the inside, then apply the outside sign.
4. Write the two-step rule.

strategy_links.why: Rapid choral or whiteboard drills build automaticity with |x| and outside-sign cases.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student ignores a sign outside the bars or negates a positive inside.
misconception_redirects.say: Do the inside first — it comes out non-negative. THEN apply any sign written outside the bars. |-7| is 7; -|7| is -7.
misconception_redirects.praise: You handled inside then outside — that's the order for absolute value.

misconception_redirects.say: Absolute value is never negative. |42| is just 42; the bars can't make it negative.
misconception_redirects.praise: You kept the absolute value non-negative.

-5 (inside first, then outside). An answer of 5 drops the outside sign.

The final value.

Distance from zero.

skills.name: Find the distance between two rationals as the absolute value of their difference
skills.i_do_script: The distance between two numbers is the absolute value of their difference: |a - b|. The absolute value guarantees a positive distance no matter which order I subtract. Watch: the distance between 3.5 and -2.5 is |3.5 - (-2.5)| = |3.5 + 2.5| = |6| = 6. Subtracting a negative turned into adding, and the bars kept it positive.

canonical_error.pattern: Drops the absolute value and reports a negative distance, or mishandles subtracting a negative
canonical_error.example: For the distance between -2.5 and 3.5 computes -2.5 - 3.5 = -6 and reports -6 as the distance, or gets 1 by mis-subtracting the negative
canonical_error.why: The student forgets that distance uses absolute value (so it's never negative) or fails to turn subtracting a negative into addition. |a - b| fixes both.

skills.item_template: Two rationals (integers, decimals, fractions), possibly same side or opposite sides of zero. Student finds |a - b|. Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: What is the distance between 3.5 and -2.5?
sample_items.distractor_logic: |3.5 - (-2.5)| = |6| = 6. Dropping the absolute value can give -6; mis-subtracting the negative gives 1.

sample_items.stem: What is the distance between -8 and 5?
What is the distance between -6 and -2?
What is the distance between 1.2 and 4.7?

redirect_script.stop: Did you wrap the difference in absolute value?
redirect_script.prompt: Distance is |a - b|. Subtract the two numbers (turning any 'minus a negative' into plus), then take the absolute value so the distance is positive.
redirect_script.praise: You subtracted and took the absolute value — a real, positive distance.

vocabulary.definition: The result of subtracting one number from another.
|a - b|, the absolute value of the difference; always non-negative.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'distance between 4 and -3 = |4 - (-3)|.'
What does 4 - (-3) become?
Subtracting -3 is adding 3: 4 + 3 = 7. Then |7| = 7. The distance is 7.
If a student writes 4 - 3 = 1, ask 'is it minus 3, or minus a negative 3? What does minus-a-negative do?'
Your turn: distance between -5 and 2.

practice_problems.stem: The distance between two numbers is written as |a - b|. Can it be negative?
practice_problems.answer: No — absolute value makes it non-negative.

practice_problems.stem: Distance between 7 and 2?
Distance between 3.5 and -2.5?
Distance between -8 and 5?
Mia found the distance between -2.5 and 3.5. Find and fix her mistake.
shown_work: Mia wrote: '-2.5 - 3.5 = -6, so the distance is -6.'
practice_problems.answer: Distance can't be negative — take the absolute value: |-2.5 - 3.5| = |-6| = 6. Mia's subtraction was fine, but she forgot the bars.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: forgetting the absolute value.

practice_problems.stem: Distance between -6 and -2?
Show that |3.5 - (-2.5)| and |-2.5 - 3.5| give the same distance.
practice_problems.answer: |3.5 + 2.5| = |6| = 6 and |-2.5 - 3.5| = |-6| = 6. Order doesn't matter after the absolute value.

practice_problems.stem: Two cities' temperatures are -4 C and 9 C. How many degrees apart are they, and write the expression you used.
practice_problems.notes: Apply the distance formula to a context.

activities.instructions:

activities.title: Don't Forget the Bars
activities.instructions:
1. Read Mia's answer of -6 for the distance between -2.5 and 3.5.

skills.name: Subtract rational numbers by adding the opposite
skills.i_do_script: Every subtraction can be rewritten as adding the opposite: a - b becomes a + (-b). This is powerful because I already know how to add signed numbers. Watch the tricky one: 2.3 - (-1.3). Adding the opposite of -1.3 is adding +1.3: 2.3 + 1.3 = 3.6. Subtracting a negative makes the result BIGGER. Another: -1 1/4 - 3 3/4 = -1 1/4 + (-3 3/4) = -5, because two negatives combine.

canonical_error.pattern: Fails to change subtraction to adding the opposite, especially when subtracting a negative
canonical_error.example: For 2.3 - (-1.3) computes 2.3 - 1.3 = 1 (treating it as subtract positive) instead of 2.3 + 1.3 = 3.6
canonical_error.why: The student ignores the second negative sign and subtracts as if the number were positive. Subtracting a negative is adding a positive: a - (-b) = a + b.

skills.item_template: A subtraction of rationals (fractions/decimals), including subtracting a negative and negative results. Numeric response.

sample_items.distractor_logic: Add the opposite: 2.3 + 1.3 = 3.6. Treating it as 2.3 - 1.3 gives 1.

redirect_script.stop: Rewrite it: subtract becomes add the ___?
redirect_script.prompt: Change a - b to a + (-b). If you're subtracting a negative, that becomes ADDING a positive. Then use your signed-addition rules.
redirect_script.praise: You added the opposite — subtraction turned into addition you already know.

vocabulary.definition: Rewrite a - b as a + (-b) to turn subtraction into addition.
a - (-b) = a + b; two minus signs make a plus.

worked_example_script.text: Rewrite the subtraction as adding the opposite. What's the opposite of -9?
Add +9: -4 + 9. Opposite signs, 9 is farther, so +5.
If a student writes -4 - 9 = -13, ask 'is it minus 9, or minus a NEGATIVE 9? Rewrite first.'
Your turn: 5 - (-2), then -2.5 - 1.5.

practice_problems.stem: Rewrite 6 - (-2) as an addition.

practice_problems.answer: Bigger (it becomes adding a positive).

practice_problems.stem: Owen evaluated 3.5 - (-2.5). Find and fix his mistake.
practice_problems.answer: Subtracting a negative is adding a positive: 3.5 - (-2.5) = 3.5 + 2.5 = 6. Owen ignored the second negative sign.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: not flipping the double negative.

practice_problems.stem: Fill in the blank: -3 - ___ = -8. Explain.
practice_problems.answer: 5 — you need -3 + (-5) = -8, so you subtract 5 (adding -5).

skills.name: Apply signed subtraction to real-world contexts
skills.i_do_script: Real-world subtraction shows up as change and as difference. A drop, a fall, or 'how much colder' means subtract. Watch: the temperature is -7 degrees and drops 5 degrees. Dropping 5 is subtracting 5: -7 - 5 = -12 degrees. For a 'difference between' question, I subtract the two values and take the absolute value if I want a positive gap. The signs come from the context: below/loss = negative, above/gain = positive.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds when the context calls for subtraction (or vice versa), or assigns the wrong sign to a value
canonical_error.why: The student misreads the direction word — a 'drop' lowers the value, so it subtracts. Direction words must be translated to the correct operation and sign before computing.

skills.item_template: A real-world change or difference problem with signed quantities. Student sets up the subtraction, computes, and interprets. Numeric response (with context).

sample_items.stem: The temperature at 1 am is -7 degrees. It drops 5 degrees over the next two hours. What is the temperature at 3 am?
A mountain peak is 1,200 m above sea level; a valley floor is 80 m below sea level. What is the difference in elevation?
A diver descends from -15 m to -40 m. How far did the diver descend?
A bank balance goes from -$30 to $45. What is the change in the balance?

redirect_script.stop: Does this word raise the value or lower it?
redirect_script.prompt: A drop, fall, or 'how much less' lowers the value — subtract. Translate the direction words to signs and to subtract-or-add, then compute. For a 'difference,' subtract and take the absolute value.
redirect_script.praise: You matched the direction word to the operation and sign — that's applying subtraction.

vocabulary.definition: How far apart two quantities are, found by subtracting (with absolute value for a positive gap).
The signed result of an ending value minus a starting value.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'Temperature -3 degrees, drops 8 degrees. New temperature?'
Does 'drops' raise or lower the temperature? Add or subtract?
Drops means subtract: -3 - 8 = -3 + (-8) = -11 degrees.
If a student writes -3 + 8 = 5, ask 'is the temperature going up or down when it drops?'
Your turn: the difference between a high of 6 C and a low of -9 C.

practice_problems.stem: Does a temperature 'drop' add or subtract?
practice_problems.answer: Subtract (it lowers the value).

practice_problems.stem: Temperature -2, drops 4. New temperature?
practice_problems.answer: -6 degrees

practice_problems.stem: Temperature -7 degrees drops 5 degrees. New temperature?
practice_problems.answer: -12 degrees

practice_problems.stem: A diver goes from -15 m to -40 m. How far did they descend?
Lia found the 3 am temperature. Find and fix her mistake.
practice_problems.answer: A drop lowers the temperature, so subtract: -7 - 5 = -12 degrees. Lia added instead of subtracting.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: adding when the context says drop.

practice_problems.stem: Difference in elevation between a peak at 1,200 m and a valley at -80 m?
The high temperature was 4 C and the low was -11 C. By how many degrees did the temperature change from high to low, and is it a rise or a fall?
practice_problems.answer: A fall of 15 degrees: -11 - 4 = -15, so 15 degrees colder.

practice_problems.stem: A submarine at -220 m rises to -60 m. Write the subtraction for the change and interpret it.
practice_problems.answer: Change = -60 - (-220) = -60 + 220 = 160 m; the submarine rose 160 m.

activities.title: Word to Operation
materials: Operation cards (subtract / add) and sign cards
activities.instructions:
1. For each situation ('drops 5 degrees', 'difference between', 'rises 3 m'), choose subtract or add and the correct signs.
2. Set up and solve the number sentence.
3. Interpret the answer's sign in context.
4. Debrief: which words signal subtraction, and which signal a negative value?

activities.title: Up or Down?
activities.instructions:
1. Read Lia's claim that -7 dropping 5 gives -2.
2. Decide whether 'drops' raises or lowers the temperature.
3. Redo it with the correct operation.
4. Write which direction words mean subtract.

content.error_step: Lia added when the temperature was dropping.

strategy_links.why: Adding-when-you-should-subtract is a precise context error a find-and-fix corrects.
A journal note mapping direction words to operations and signs consolidates the translation.
Think-pair-share on 'is this a rise or a fall' builds interpretation of the signed result.

Should you add or subtract here?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student adds when the context describes a drop/fall, or assigns the wrong sign.
misconception_redirects.say: A drop, fall, or 'how much less' lowers the value — subtract. Translate the direction words to signs and to subtract-or-add, then compute. For a 'difference,' subtract and take the absolute value.
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched the direction word to the operation and sign — that's applying subtraction.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student gives a negative 'difference' for a distance-apart question.

quick_checks.look_for: -10. An answer of 2 diagnoses adding instead of subtracting.
13 (|5 - (-8)|). An answer of -3 or 3 means the double negative was mishandled.

worked_solution.stem: The temperature at dusk is -2 degrees. Overnight it drops 9 degrees. What is the temperature by dawn?

steps.annotation: Translate the direction word to an operation.
Start at -2, subtract the 9-degree drop.
Add the opposite; two negatives combine.
Colder than the start, as a drop should be.

faded_example.stem: A hiker at 60 m elevation descends to -25 m (below a canyon rim marked as 0). How far did the hiker descend?

steps.annotation: Difference of the two elevations.
Subtract the starting elevation.
Take the absolute value for a positive distance.
State how far the hiker descended.

skills.name: Reason about differences and distance with variables
skills.i_do_script: Sometimes I reason about a - b = c from where a and b sit on the number line, without exact values. Key ideas: |a - b| is the distance between them, so it's never negative. If a is to the RIGHT of b, then a - b is positive; if a is to the LEFT, a - b is negative. Watch: if a is at -1 and b is at 4, then a - b = -1 - 4 = -5, which is negative because a is left of b, and its size 5 is the distance between them.

canonical_error.pattern: Confuses the sign of the difference with the distance, or misjudges which of a, b is larger
canonical_error.example: For a left of b on the number line, claims a - b > 0 (because 'a comes first'), instead of a - b < 0
canonical_error.why: The student uses position order rather than value order. a - b is positive only when a is greater (to the right of) b; the distance |a - b| is always the positive gap regardless of order.

skills.item_template: An abstract a - b = c statement with a, b positioned on a number line; student selects true statements about c's sign and magnitude. MC/multi-select.

sample_items.stem: On a number line, a is to the LEFT of b (a < b). The difference a - b = c. Which is true about c?
sample_items.distractor_logic: If a < b, then a - b is negative. The distance is |a - b| = |c|, not c itself.

sample_items.stem: For any two different numbers a and b, what does |a - b| represent?
sample_items.distractor_logic: |a - b| is the distance, non-negative and independent of order.

sample_items.stem: If a - b = 0, what must be true about a and b?
sample_items.answer: a = b (they are the same number)
choices: a = b (they are the same number)
sample_items.distractor_logic: A zero difference means a and b are equal, so their distance apart is 0.

sample_items.stem: a is at 3 and b is at -2. Which is true? (a) a - b = 5  (b) b - a = 5  (c) |a - b| = 5
sample_items.answer: a - b = 5 and |a - b| = 5 are both true
choices: a - b = 5 and |a - b| = 5 are both true
sample_items.distractor_logic: a - b = 3 - (-2) = 5 (positive since a > b); |a - b| = 5; b - a = -5, not 5.

redirect_script.stop: Which is bigger, a or b — not which comes first?
redirect_script.prompt: The sign of a - b comes from VALUE order: a - b is positive when a is greater (right of) b, negative when a is smaller. The distance |a - b| is always the positive gap, either way.
redirect_script.praise: You judged the sign by value order and the distance by absolute value — that's the full picture.

vocabulary.definition: a - b is positive when a > b, negative when a < b, zero when a = b.
|a - b|, the non-negative gap between a and b.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for 7.NS.3 (products of rational numbers) and 8.NS.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'a is at -3, b is at 2. Find a - b and |a - b|.'
Is a greater or less than b? So is a - b positive or negative?
a < b, so a - b is negative: -3 - 2 = -5. The distance |a - b| = 5, the gap between them.
If a student says a - b is positive because a is written first, ask 'which number is actually bigger?'
Your turn: if a - b = 0, what does that say about a and b?

practice_problems.stem: What does |a - b| always represent?
practice_problems.answer: The distance between a and b (never negative).

practice_problems.stem: If a - b = 0, how are a and b related?
practice_problems.answer: They are equal (a = b).

practice_problems.stem: a is left of b on the number line (a < b). Is a - b positive or negative?
practice_problems.answer: Negative (a < b).
practice_problems.notes: Sign from value order, not position order.

practice_problems.stem: a is at 3, b is at -2. Find a - b and |a - b|.
practice_problems.notes: a > b so difference is positive and equals the distance.

practice_problems.stem: Reed reasoned about a - b for a to the left of b. Find and fix his statement.
shown_work: Reed wrote: 'a comes first, so a - b must be positive.'
practice_problems.answer: The sign depends on which VALUE is bigger, not which is written first. If a is to the left (a < b), then a - b is negative. Reed used position order instead of value order.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: position order vs value order.

practice_problems.stem: For a = -5 and b = -1, find a - b and the distance |a - b|.
practice_problems.notes: Both negative; a < b so difference is negative.

practice_problems.stem: Explain why |a - b| = |b - a| for any a and b.
practice_problems.answer: a - b and b - a are opposites (same size, opposite sign), and absolute value ignores sign, so both give the same distance.

practice_problems.stem: If |a - b| = 6 and a = 2, what are the possible values of b?
practice_problems.answer: b = 8 or b = -4, since both are 6 units from 2.
practice_problems.notes: Use distance to find unknown positions.

activities.title: Sign of the Difference
materials: Cards describing a and b positions with claims about a - b
activities.instructions:
1. Each card gives the positions of a and b and a claim about a - b or |a - b|.
2. Sort into 'True' and 'False.'
3. Justify each with value order (for the sign) or distance (for the magnitude).
4. Debrief: how do you decide the sign of a - b, and how do you decide the distance?

cards.text: a - b = 0 -> a and b are opposites

activities.title: Value Order, Not Position
activities.instructions:
1. Read Reed's claim that a - b is positive because 'a comes first.'
2. Pick values with a to the left of b (like a = -1, b = 4) and compute a - b.
3. Decide the true sign and explain using value order.
4. Write the rule for the sign of a - b.

content.worked_problem: a to the left of b. Reed said a - b > 0 because a comes first.
content.error_step: Reed used the written order instead of value order.
content.why: a < b means a - b < 0; e.g., -1 - 4 = -5.

strategy_links.why: Think-pair-share on abstract a - b statements surfaces the value-order-vs-position reasoning for debate.
The position-order error is a precise generalization a counterexample corrects.
Journaling the rule for the sign of a difference consolidates the abstract reasoning.

questioning_prompts: Which value is bigger, a or b — not which is written first?
So is a - b positive or negative?
What does |a - b| represent no matter the order?
If a - b = 0, what must be true about a and b?
Why does |a - b| = |b - a|?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student judges the sign of a - b by which variable is written first.
misconception_redirects.say: The sign of a - b comes from VALUE order: a - b is positive when a is greater (right of) b, negative when a is smaller. The distance |a - b| is always the positive gap, either way.
misconception_redirects.praise: You judged the sign by value order and the distance by absolute value — that's the full picture.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student says a - b = 0 means a and b are opposites.
misconception_redirects.say: A zero difference means a and b are EQUAL, not opposite. Opposites sum to zero; equal numbers subtract to zero.
misconception_redirects.praise: You separated 'difference is zero' (equal) from 'sum is zero' (opposite).

quick_checks.look_for: Negative (a < b; -4 - 1 = -5). 'Positive' means position order was used.

quick_checks.prompt: If a - b = 0, how are a and b related?
quick_checks.look_for: Equal (a = b). 'Opposites' confuses difference with sum.

looking_back.label: Looking Back
looking_back.description: Skills the student should have but may need re-teaching.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S4 (subtract rationals by adding the opposite) -- the At-proficiency computational engine and the source of the double-negative error. If they pass, move to S3 (distance as |a - b|), S5 (real-world subtraction), and S6 (reasoning). If they fail, drop to S1/S2 to check whether absolute value itself is understood. S3 doubles as a branch check on the distance principle.
